atlas-bg.0068: No national graduate season was found; hiring runs all year, with fairs and monthly job exchanges as peaks. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0069: The routes found, centres, portals and academies, ask for skills and languages rather than a master’s. This is our reading; no employer page states a degree level.
atlas-bg.0070: After the first review employers often ask for translated and authenticated education certificates; the Employment Agency also wants education documents authenticated by the issuing country, and Bulgarian programmes need a legal Bulgarian translation.
atlas-bg.0071: NACID, the national academic recognition centre, handles foreign diplomas and publishes a list of regulated professions, which need recognition.
atlas-bg.0072: The routes that employ most juniors, the academies and the centres, are skills-based, and no page read ranks universities. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0073: We found no apprenticeship or dual-study route to graduate jobs; the structured routes are academies and the Youth Guarantee. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0074: We found no figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hiring in Bulgaria; the Employment Agency lists vacancies centrally but does not break them down. “Medium” is a placeholder reading.
atlas-bg.0075: A non-EU hire needs the employer to advertise the vacancy at the Employment Agency for at least 15 days, and non-EU staff may not exceed 20% of the workforce (35% in small and medium firms); EU Blue Card hires are exempt from the test and the cap. See Visas for the rules.
atlas-bg.0076: A photo is usual on Bulgarian CVs; no page read states the norm, and Career Show runs a CV photo studio at its Sofia fair. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0077: EURES recommends the Europass CV format; it states no page limit, so two pages is our reading of what is usual.
atlas-bg.0078: Employers usually expect a brief cover letter with the CV.
atlas-bg.0079: After the first review employers often ask for more documents, including references from former employers.
atlas-bg.0080: Prepare translated and authenticated education certificates and proof of work experience; employers ask for them after the first review.
atlas-bg.0081: No page read says whether a salary expectation is asked in the application; Rivermate says offers should be market-related and mix base pay with benefits. Our reading is that pay is raised later.
atlas-bg.0082: Employers asking for references from former employers is the only check found; we found nothing on background checks. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0083: Portals, fairs and academies take open applications, while outside the international centres introductions count. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0084: Centres recruit in English and applications are online; Rivermate says onboarding takes one to two weeks, and up to four months when immigration is involved.
atlas-bg.0085: English in international centres; Bulgarian elsewhere, and employment contracts must be written in Bulgarian.
atlas-bg.0086: Progress’s internship in Sofia has three steps: a CV (a portfolio or repository link is highly recommended), a HackerRank assignment of about 90 minutes to be finished within five days of the invitation, and an onsite interview of 75–90 minutes with several Progress professionals, covering technical and behavioural questions.
atlas-bg.0087: We found no page describing the selection stages of the finance and business-process centres, nor the usual time from application to offer or dress norms; general practice there is an interview with a language check. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0088: After the first review, employers often ask for more documents: translated and authenticated education certificates, proof of experience and references from former employers.
atlas-bg.0089: A written employment contract is mandatory and must be concluded before you start; it must be in Bulgarian. The employer notifies the National Revenue Agency within three days and gives you a copy, and you can start only after registration.
atlas-bg.0090: Probation can last up to six months, and during it a worker may be dismissed without prior notice; for fixed-term contracts under one year it cannot exceed one month. After probation the notice is one month for an indefinite contract and three months for a fixed-term one.
atlas-bg.0091: The standard week is five days and at most 40 hours. Rivermate says two-thirds of companies pay bonuses, though they are not mandatory. We did not establish whether graduates negotiate or how long employers give to decide.
atlas-bg.0092: The employer must run a labour-market test by advertising the vacancy at the Employment Agency for at least 15 days, unless the job is on the shortage-occupations list, and the Agency gives an opinion (fee €51.13) before the single permit is issued.
atlas-bg.0093: Non-EU staff may not exceed 20% of a firm’s average annual workforce (35% for small and medium firms). EU Blue Card hires are exempt from the test and the cap but need a contract of at least six months at 1.5 times the average gross wage, which the library puts at €2,166 gross a month in 2026.
atlas-bg.0094: Ask early: Rivermate says onboarding takes up to four months when immigration is involved. Which employers actually sponsor, and what they want to hear, was not established; the international centres are the likely ones. This is our reading.
atlas-bg.0095: Portals named by EURES: jobs.bg, karieri.bg, zaplata.bg, jobtiger.bg, rabota.bg; the Employment Agency’s site (az.government.bg) and the EURES job-mobility portal; company websites, especially in IT and business-process outsourcing.
atlas-bg.0096: Bulgarian EURES advisers give information in English, German, Spanish and French; registration at the Employment Agency’s local job centres is free.
atlas-bg.0097: Career Show Bulgaria (careershow.bg) for fairs, Telerik Academy and SoftUni for developer training, and AIBEST (aibest.org), the outsourcing industry association, for member companies and events.
atlas-bg.0098: Arriving without translated and authenticated education certificates: employers ask for them right after the first review, and Bulgarian programmes need a legal Bulgarian translation of foreign diplomas.
atlas-bg.0099: Starting work before the contract is written and registered: the contract must be concluded in writing before the first day, and the employee can start only after registration.
atlas-bg.0100: Assuming English is enough everywhere: the centres recruit in English, but contracts must be in Bulgarian and elsewhere the working language is Bulgarian.
atlas-bg.0101: Waiting for the autumn to look for a summer internship: Progress’s applications open on 20 April and TechnoLogica’s 2026 deadline was 22 June.
atlas-bg.0102: Skipping the cover letter: employers usually expect a brief one.
atlas-bg.0103: Finance, accounting and HR centres recruit in English, while contracts must be in Bulgarian and local employers work in Bulgarian. Rivermate notes that Bulgarian workers often speak German, French and Nordic languages, which the centres value. The level and the evidence asked for (certificate, interview) were not established.
atlas-bg.0104: Bank jobs, such as UniCredit Bulbank or First Investment Bank in Sofia, work in Bulgarian; English is the language of the international finance centres. We read no listing stating a level.
atlas-bg.0105: Progress’s internship asks for very good written and spoken English and tests it in the interview; no certificate or CEFR level is named. Telerik Academy and SoftUni train in programming and say their graduates are hired by technology companies.
atlas-bg.0106: Eurostat counted 90.0% of Bulgarian tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within three years as in work in 2025 (EU 85.3%), with youth unemployment of 13.1%: graduates are in demand, but this is a national figure that says nothing about the quality of the first job.
atlas-bg.0107: Progress states that more than 75% of its technical interns have received job offers after the internship, depending on performance and business needs; it is the employer’s own figure for all its offices, not for Sofia alone.
atlas-bg.0108: Telerik Academy says 68% of its graduates were employed within two months of finishing, and SoftUni says 97% of its programming alumni started a tech job; both are the schools’ own figures with no stated method.
atlas-bg.0109: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens work on equal terms with Bulgarians, with no permit or visa.
atlas-bg.0110: Staying over three months, register with the Migration Directorate of your area within three months, with your registered contract or enrolment and proof of housing; the certificate is issued the same day.
atlas-bg.0111: Bulgaria uses the euro since 1 January 2026.
atlas-bg.0113: The university sends your file to the Ministry of Education, which issues the certificate of admission; then the D visa, and a one-year permit renewed each year of the course.
atlas-bg.0114: Work 20 hours a week in term and full time in holidays, with no separate permit: the employer registers the job with the employment agency within seven working days.
atlas-bg.0115: A non-EU student with a permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days with no Bulgarian visa or permit, on the university’s notification.
atlas-bg.0116: €7,442.40 a year (12 times the minimum wage)
atlas-bg.0121: For graduates of the last two years or students abroad: an employment contract with a traineeship clause, a mentor with three years’ experience and a training programme, for 6 to 12 months, paid at least the minimum wage.
atlas-bg.0122: Students enrolled in Bulgaria do the internship of their degree with no work authorisation.
atlas-bg.0124: Nine months to look for work or start a business
atlas-bg.0125: After a Bulgarian degree or research project: nine months, not extendable. A job or company then converts it inside Bulgaria, with no new visa and no labour-market test.
